summary:
Samoa's Crimes Act 2013 (Tulafono o Solitulafono 2013), in force 1 May 2013, criminalises same-sex sexual conduct through sections 67, 68 and 71. Section 67 makes the offence complete on penetration with no defence of consent, section 68 makes attempts liable to imprisonment for up to five years, and section 71 makes keeping a place of resort for homosexual acts liable to up to seven years. The Human Dignity Trust country profile records the headline penalty as five years. The same sections also prohibit heterosexual anal intercourse and oral sex.

The 2007 decision Police v Poi defined the act as penetration of the anus by the offender's penis, whether of a male or female victim. Because the offence is framed by the sexual act rather than by the partners' identity, it reaches a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship, and on that definition it also reaches anal intercourse with a female partner. Samoa should be treated as a jurisdiction where same-sex conduct remains on the statute book.

The overview source states that the law is not enforced, and the inventory records no prosecution under sections 67, 68 or 71. In June 2010 the Samoa Law Reform Commission recommended repealing all criminal penalties for sodomy and related acts in private between consenting adult males, reporting majority public support; the Government rejected that recommendation and a reported 2011 decriminalisation proposal. The provisions remain in force.

The Crimes Act 2013 also removed the former Crimes Ordinance 1961 provisions that criminalised males "impersonating" females in a public place, which had been used to target transgender women and gender-diverse people. RNZ Pacific reported on 3 May 2013 that Samoa Fa'afafine Association president To'oto'oali'i Roger Stanley expressed relief at the removal, and that the community was not then agitating to repeal the sodomy provisions. Gender presentation as such is no longer an offence.

Section 7(1)(h) of the Sentencing Act 2016 (Tulafono o Faasalaga 2016) provides for crimes motivated by gender identity, and for crimes motivated by sexual orientation, at sentencing. As a provision of a sentencing statute it operates at the sentencing stage of a separately charged offence rather than as a standalone charge.

The Mental Health Act 2007, published 2 February 2007, states that people are not to be considered mentally ill if they refuse or fail to express a particular sexual orientation, and prohibits conversion therapy by mental health professionals.

Samoa does not recognise same-sex relationships. Prime-ministerial statements in 2012, 2013 and 2017 rejected same-sex marriage on Christian and traditional grounds.

In the UN Universal Periodic Review Samoa rejected first-cycle recommendations from Canada, France and Norway to repeal criminalisation, and rejected all second-cycle recommendations except Slovenia's on reducing violence, stating that decriminalisation was not possible because of cultural sensitivities and Christian beliefs. In 2011 Samoa signed the UN joint statement on ending acts of violence and related human rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity. The Ombudsman's first National State of Human Rights Report, released in August 2015, referred to fa'afafine as "the third gender that has always existed in Samoa". In the UPR process the government stated that fa'afafine, gays and lesbians were integral members of society and heirs to family chiefly titles and lands through extended family consensus, while describing sexual orientation as a sensitive issue requiring education and sensitisation for acceptance.

Fa'afafine, meaning people assigned male at birth who embody both gender traits, and fa'afatama, people assigned female at birth who embody both gender traits, have been recognised as gender identities or gender roles in Samoa since at least the early 20th century. The overview source characterises Samoan society as very tolerant of being transgender but not of homosexuality, and describes Samoa as fairly progressive on gender identity and expression because of the size of its fa'afafine community. Samoa held its first LGBTQ Pride Week in 2026, with LGBTQ residents and allies gathering to celebrate the community.
tangentialFactors:
APTN reported on 9 May 2024 that a convening in Nadi, Fiji gathered gender-diverse community members from Samoa, Cook Islands, Vanuatu, Kiribati, Fiji, Tonga, West Papua and Papua New Guinea, documenting the regional MVPFAFF+ spectrum of identities that Samoa's fa'afafine community belongs to alongside fakaleiti in Tonga and fakafifine in Niue. The convening shows an organised regional network, but it is a meeting record rather than evidence about conditions inside Samoa.

Schmidt's 2001 academic article in Intersections, "Redefining Fa'afafine: Western Discourses and the Construction of Transgenderism in Samoa", analyses fa'afafine as "in the manner of a woman" and argues that the identity is both viewed through and reshaped by Western sexuality and transgenderism discourses, with Auckland's Samoan diaspora as a contact zone. This bears on how the term is likely to be encountered and translated by a visitor, not on legal exposure.

The UN Free & Equal Pacific information sheet of August 2015 lists the fa'afafine of Samoa, American Samoa and Tokelau among diverse pre-colonial Pacific gender identities described as important parts of the cultural treasure of the region. The Samoa Fa'afafine Association's stakeholder report for Samoa's third-cycle UPR in 2021 describes the culturally unique third-gender identities fa'afafine and fa'atama and documents lived experiences, aiming to establish grounds for non-discriminatory policy and legislation.

Censorship decisions show official selectivity toward gender and sexuality content rather than a rule bearing on visitors: in 2009 the Censorship Board banned screening of the film Milk about gay activist Harvey Milk while allowing Lesbian Vampire Killers, and in 2019 banned Rocketman about Elton John. The decisions were criticised as hypocritical, ignorant and an exercise in selective morality and were protested by the Samoa Fa'afafine Association.

The inventory contains no trans-specific violence figure for Samoa, no count of incidents and no denominator, so no comparison with the general homicide rate can be drawn and none should be inferred from the absence of figures.
localsOnly:
Section 20(2) of the Labour and Employment Relations Act 2013 prohibits direct and indirect discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in employment policies, procedures or practices. Section 7(1)(h) of the Sentencing Act 2016 likewise covers crimes motivated by sexual orientation. Neither provision is stated in the inventory to cover gender identity in employment.

The Samoa Fa'afafine Association is described as fostering collaboration between the fa'afafine and LGBTQ communities and promoting a positive attitude toward the Samoan fa'afafine community while balancing Samoan values with Western influences. It regards anti-gay laws as hindering the full incorporation of both fa'afafine and gay and lesbian Samoans, stated in 2017 that its priority was the promotion of human rights and the reduction of discrimination and violence based on gender identity, and stated in 2018 that marriage was the least of its worries when people do not have a job.

Fa'afafine and fa'afatama hold family chiefly titles and lands through extended family consensus, according to the government's own UPR statements, which places third-gender people inside the matai system in a way that is not mirrored in the statute book.

The conversion therapy prohibition in the Mental Health Act 2007 binds mental health professionals, and the act's provision on sexual orientation addresses diagnosis rather than gender identity; the inventory does not source a gender-identity equivalent in that statute.
outOfScopeNotes:
A Reuters feature on Samoa's third gender balancing sex and religion returned HTTP 401 at research time and could not be read, so its content is unresolved rather than assessed.

The APTN socio-economic study covering Samoa is published as a scanned image document, so its findings could not be extracted and remain unresolved.

The inventory contains no entry, visa, passport-marker, border-screening or airport-secondary-screening claim for Samoa, and none has been supplied here; a traveller's document and screening exposure is not sourced either way.

The statement that the law is not enforced comes from a public encyclopedia overview without case-level citation, and no prosecution search or official non-enforcement policy is documented in the inventory. Whether sections 67, 68 and 71 have been used in the period since 2013 is unresolved.

The characterisation that Samoan society is very tolerant of being transgender but not of homosexuality carries no survey, population surveyed, category measured or period in the inventory, so its magnitude and currency are unresolved.

The 2026 Pride Week is sourced only to the same public encyclopedia overview and is not corroborated in the inventory by primary or contemporaneous reporting.
